items.title: Ochaworth — Purpose, made visible
items.description: A four-month design and development project translating a community initiative’s mission, programmes and opportunities to participate into a connected website.

caseStudy.tools: React, TypeScript, React Router, Tailwind CSS, Vite, Netlify Forms, Netlify Functions
caseStudy.summary: I designed and developed the website for Ochaworth Leadership and Community Development Initiative over four months. The project brings the organisation’s advocacy, programmes and community activities together, with clear routes to learn more, volunteer, apply for membership and stay in touch.
caseStudy.coverAlt: Ochaworth case-study cover in plum, magenta and orange with original community-walk imagery.
caseStudy.coverCaption: Portfolio cover using the website’s implemented theme and original campaign imagery. Supporting layout studies below are labelled separately from website photography.

sections.heading: The project at a glance
sections.body:
Ochaworth Leadership and Community Development Initiative presents itself as a youth-led organisation advancing women’s and girls’ rights, health, equality and human dignity in Nigeria. Its website needs to introduce that work and help people understand how they can participate.

I designed and developed the site over four months. The scope includes the homepage, organisational information, programmes, gallery, blog, contact, volunteer and membership journeys, supported by a shared visual system and reusable React components.

sections.heading: The challenge: connect a broad mission to clear actions
sections.body:
The organisation’s work spans several themes, from women’s leadership and menstrual dignity to cancer awareness and support for vulnerable communities. A visitor needs a way to understand those themes without reading every page before finding a relevant action.

I approached the website as a sequence: introduce the mission, show the work, provide context, then offer a route to participate. Programme information, campaign photography and repeated calls to action connect the organisation’s message with practical next steps.

sections.heading: A visual language with warmth and presence
sections.body:
The implemented theme combines magenta, plum and orange with light content surfaces. Darker sections create emphasis, while the orange accent distinguishes important actions and highlighted words. Photography supplies the human context behind the organisation’s message.

Playfair Display gives major headings an editorial character; Poppins carries navigation, body copy and controls. Rounded cards, generous section spacing and consistent button styles connect pages that contain different kinds of information.

images.caption: Visual-system study based on the website’s theme configuration and font choices.
images.alt: Magenta, plum, orange and off-white colour palette with editorial heading and interface typography.

sections.heading: The homepage: lead with purpose, then open a path
sections.body:
The hero combines campaign imagery, a short mission-led headline and supporting text. Donate and Learn More offer two different levels of commitment: act on an existing interest or first understand the organisation. A rotating presentation introduces different campaign themes within the same opening structure.

The following participation cards introduce volunteering and community involvement. Rather than making the visitor search through the footer for every action, the homepage places opportunities to engage near the organisation’s main story.

The cover for this case study uses photography already published on the website. It is a portfolio presentation of the project, rather than a browser capture.

sections.heading: Explain the organisation before asking for deeper involvement
sections.body:
The About content pairs a collage of community images with a concise introduction and supporting themes. A dedicated About page expands this into mission, vision and values. This separates the quick overview needed on the homepage from the fuller context available to interested visitors.

The website also includes organisational statements and impact figures. Those are content supplied by the site; I have not treated them as independently verified findings or as performance outcomes of my design work.

sections.heading: Programme discovery: turn themes into understandable projects
sections.body:
Programme cards pair imagery with a name, location or supporting context and a route to learn more. The dedicated programmes page distinguishes ongoing, upcoming and completed work, so visitors can understand whether an initiative is active or documented as past activity.

Programme details make space for descriptions, objectives, context, imagery and other supporting information. The structure can accommodate different initiatives without forcing every programme into a single long homepage description.

images.caption: Programme-content hierarchy study using published campaign names and website imagery. This is an illustrative layout, not a screenshot.
images.alt: Two illustrative programme cards for Pad A Girl Child and World Cancer Day Walk, showing status, title, context and next action.

sections.heading: Showing the work through original campaign imagery
sections.body:
The site’s programme and gallery images put people and activities alongside the written mission. The published Pad A Girl Child content concerns menstrual-health education and dignity; the World Cancer Day Walk content introduces awareness and community action.

These examples explain the kind of information the website brings together. The case study uses the organisation’s existing imagery as project material without presenting campaign targets, participant counts or fundraising figures as website results.

images.caption: Original image used by the website for its Pad A Girl Child programme.
images.alt: Published Ochaworth programme photograph from the Pad A Girl Child content.

images.caption: Original image used by the website for World Cancer Day Walk.
images.alt: Published Ochaworth photograph from the World Cancer Day Walk content.

sections.heading: Several audiences, several routes to participate
sections.body:
A person who wants to read about the organisation has a different task from someone applying to volunteer. I separated these paths through dedicated About, Programmes, Volunteer, membership and contact pages, while keeping shared navigation and footer links across the site.

The volunteer and membership application forms provide distinct destinations. Gallery, blog and newsletter content give visitors another way to stay connected when they are interested in the work but are not ready to apply or contribute.

images.caption: A route map based on the implemented navigation and page structure.
images.alt: Routes for learning about Ochaworth, exploring programmes, applying to participate and staying connected.

sections.heading: Forms: make the next step feel acknowledged
sections.body:
Contact, membership, volunteer and newsletter forms connect the public-facing pages with Netlify Forms. Static form definitions allow Netlify’s build process to recognise submissions even though the visible interfaces are rendered by React.

The source also includes separate Netlify Functions for confirmation emails. For contact and application forms, the email step follows the form submission, so the acknowledgment email is distinct from the submission itself. This separates the essential action from a courtesy follow-up.

These are implementation details confirmed in the source. I have not submitted real applications or tested live email delivery as part of preparing this case study.

sections.heading: The donation interface: distinguish intent from completion
sections.body:
The homepage includes a donation interface with preset amounts, a custom amount field, contact fields and cause selection. This gives the intended contribution journey a clear visual structure.

In the reviewed implementation, the form changes to a thank-you state in the browser; I did not find a completed payment-processing step in that handler. This case study therefore describes the donation interface as designed, rather than claiming verified payment collection or funds raised through the website.

A complete contribution journey would need payment integration, reliable server-side recording and a confirmation tied to the actual payment result.

sections.heading: Development: a consistent system across content-rich pages
sections.body:
React and TypeScript organise the interface into page components and shared elements. React Router handles the different destinations, while reusable buttons, section labels, newsletter components and the main layout maintain consistency. Tailwind CSS supports responsive grids, spacing and interface states.

Vite provides the build setup, and Netlify hosts the website and its form and function integrations. Text, programme information and theme values are separated into structured data files, allowing content updates without rewriting the page components.

Responsive rules shift the navigation and multi-column sections for smaller screens. This describes the implemented approach; a rendered mobile usability review was not part of this case-study preparation.

sections.heading: The outcome and the next questions
sections.body:
The delivered website gives Ochaworth a connected presentation of its mission, programmes and ways to get involved. Visitors can move from the homepage to organisational context, programme details, community imagery and dedicated participation forms.

The evidence here is the delivered website, its published content and its implementation. I am not claiming a measured increase in donations, applications, traffic or engagement, or a formal user-research result.

The next useful evaluation would examine whether visitors can find a relevant programme, understand the difference between volunteering and membership, complete forms on mobile and receive clear feedback. Completing and verifying the payment journey would be another priority before describing online donations as a finished capability.

The project reinforced a practical design lesson: an organisation’s mission becomes easier to engage with when its content, visual hierarchy and participation paths tell the same story.

items.title: Kuppid — Designed for real connection
items.description: A two-month design and development project bringing discovery, mutual matching, messaging and member support into one dating platform for adults across Nigeria.

caseStudy.tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Supabase, Firebase Hosting, Paystack, Brevo
caseStudy.summary: I designed and developed Kuppid, a dating platform for adults across Nigeria. Over two months, I worked across its brand, public website, member experience and admin tools—connecting the first visit to profile creation, discovery, mutual matching and conversation.

sections.heading: The project at a glance
sections.body:
Kuppid brings the public website and the signed-in dating experience together. The public site introduces the product; the app lets members create a profile, discover people, express interest and talk after a mutual match. Behind the scenes, an admin dashboard supports member management, reports, payments and email communication.

My role covered both design and development. That meant taking responsibility for how the experience looked, how the different journeys connected and how the product behaved when something went wrong. The project took two months.

sections.heading: The challenge: make connection feel approachable
sections.body:
A dating platform asks people to share personal information before they know whether the experience will be worthwhile. The design therefore needed to answer practical questions early: What am I joining? How do matching and messaging work? What stays private? What can I do if I feel uncomfortable?

I treated clarity as a product requirement. The goal was a connected journey with understandable actions, visible feedback and accessible routes to support, rather than a collection of attractive screens.

sections.heading: A visual identity with warmth and confidence
sections.body:
The interlocking heart-link mark expresses connection without relying on a generic heart alone. Violet anchors the interface, pale yellow adds warmth, and lavender surfaces keep the experience light. Dark text maintains hierarchy across cards and forms.

Bricolage Grotesque ExtraBold gives the brand and major headings a distinctive voice. Rounded controls and profile cards carry that warmth into the product, while familiar labels and consistent spacing keep actions readable.

images.caption: A design-system study based on Kuppid’s implemented palette, headline typography and primary actions.
images.alt: Kuppid palette, headline typography and signup and Android actions.

sections.heading: The landing page: start with a clear invitation
sections.body:
The hero leads with “Find your person. Feel the connection.” The message is broad enough for a product open across Nigeria rather than tying the service to one city. Supporting copy explains the purpose before asking visitors to act.

The hero has two actions: create a free profile and download for Android. Login remains in the main navigation. The free allowance sits close to the signup decision, with no card required to start. This creates a clear hierarchy without asking visitors to choose among several competing hero buttons.

images.caption: Landing-page hierarchy study using Kuppid’s copy and original marketing imagery. This is a layout study rather than a browser screenshot.
images.alt: Kuppid hero, signup and Android buttons, four-step explanation and landing-page content sequence.

sections.heading: Explain the journey before asking for commitment
sections.body:
“Good things start simply” breaks the experience into a short sequence: create a profile, discover people, establish mutual interest and start a conversation. This gives visitors a mental model before they enter the app.

The “A look inside” section then illustrates discovery, shared reasons and messaging. Demo profiles are explicitly labelled fictional. The previews show what the product does without presenting invented member stories as social proof. Animated details inside the preview cards add life while the cards themselves stay in place. Reduced-motion preferences are respected.

sections.heading: Shared interests give people a reason to say hello
sections.body:
The discovery and shared-interest sections move beyond the idea of simply browsing photos. They introduce interests and dating intentions as useful context for deciding whether to connect.

Inside the app, discovery filters and “Show me” preferences help shape the people a member sees. “Why you match” provides shared reasons: a free preview is available, while Premium reveals the fuller explanation. The case-study cover uses illustrative mockups; it should not be read as an exact capture of every production screen.

images.caption: The core member journey and recovery paths, mapped from the implemented product.
images.alt: Flow from signup to discovery, mutual match and conversation, with recovery paths.

sections.heading: Safety belongs in the main story
sections.body:
The landing page makes space for boundaries and personal comfort. Its message that people do not owe anyone a conversation supports the product’s unmatch, block and report actions. These routes matter as much as the invitation to connect.

The product distinguishes email verification from photo verification; photo review remains a future update rather than a claim the current experience can make. Profile privacy controls, hidden-area options and support access make privacy and recovery part of the normal journey.

sections.heading: FAQs, pricing and Android access remove uncertainty
sections.body:
FAQs answer the questions that can prevent someone from starting: whether an app download is required, who the service is for, where it is available, who can see a profile and how to stop a conversation. Local coverage is explained without inventing community counts or guaranteeing a match nearby.

The pricing page separates the free plan from paid benefits. Free members receive five likes per day and no daily picks. Premium adds unlimited likes, daily picks and plan-specific extras. Payments are one-time purchases without automatic renewal; a new plan can be queued after an existing subscription ends.

The Android section provides a direct download and installation steps, while browser access remains available. The public website and app are separate destinations, connected through signup, login and download actions.

sections.heading: From a saved profile to a useful discovery experience
sections.body:
Profile creation collects the information needed for discovery, including dating intention, interests and preferences. Completion and photo requirements are enforced by the backend, with instructions in the interface when information is missing.

Empty states matter here. Reaching the end of a list should not look like the app has failed. The interface gives members a way to review preferences, refresh discovery or come back as the community grows. Visibility controls let people pause discovery when they need a break.

sections.heading: Messaging: show what changed without making people search
sections.body:
An important iteration addressed incoming messages that did not become obvious until a member opened the conversation. The inbox now exposes unread counts and previews, and puts the conversation with the newest message first. Profile-led cards preserve the visual style while making activity easier to scan.

Conversation tools include replies, edits, reactions and optional disappearing messages. Read-state consistency and attachment failure handling were part of the implementation work. The purpose is simple: members should understand what arrived, what was read and what action is available next.

images.caption: An illustrative interaction study of inbox priority, unread cues and conversation tools. Names and messages are fictional.
images.alt: Fictional inbox cards with unread badges and a private conversation with message bubbles.

sections.heading: Designing the tools needed to run the product
sections.body:
The admin dashboard brings together members, support, community activity, Premium and referral management. Operational views use counts where conversation contents are unnecessary, and permissions control which team members can access each area.

Support replies can be composed by email inside the dashboard rather than opening a separate mailbox. Email delivery reporting distinguishes provider acceptance from confirmed delivery. Welcome emails and birthday messages extend the product experience beyond the app, with wording and delivery handled as part of the broader service.

The work also included investigating profile-photo upload failures and improving feedback around errors. These operational details are part of the experience: a member’s journey continues when they need help.

sections.heading: Development: turn design decisions into enforceable behavior
sections.body:
The interface uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Supabase supports authentication, database access, storage and server-side functions, while Firebase Hosting serves the website and app. Paystack handles payments and Brevo supports app email delivery.

Important product rules belong on the server. For example, free-like allowances and Premium-only daily picks are enforced in the database rather than relying on a disabled button. Member-facing controls are paired with backend authorization and privacy checks.

Testing covered areas such as messaging, support replies, account changes, upload behavior and Premium access. A regression run during the documented work passed 108 tests, alongside targeted database checks. That is implementation evidence, not a claim that the product is bug-free or that conversion improved.

sections.heading: Iteration: clarity is a design decision
sections.body:
Several refinements came from specific feedback and observed issues. The original hero was restored above the product previews when a content change disrupted the page hierarchy. A duplicate city-guide link was removed from the hero, and the hero actions were reduced to signup and Android download, with login in navigation.

Messaging retained profile cards while gaining unread counts, previews and newest-first ordering. Discovery-filter alignment and form feedback were also reviewed. These changes show how presentation and functionality need to be evaluated together: adding a useful feature should not obscure an existing journey.

sections.heading: The outcome and what comes next
sections.body:
The delivered product connects a branded public website with a working member app and the tools needed to operate it. The work spans acquisition, account setup, discovery, matching, messaging, payments and support.

No conversion lift, retention improvement or formal usability-study result is claimed here. The case study focuses on the product delivered, the reasoning behind its design and the implementation issues addressed. Future evaluation should examine profile-completion drop-off, first-match and first-conversation journeys, mobile usability and support resolution.

My main takeaway was that a dating experience depends on clear expectations as much as visual appeal. The invitation, the first action, the feedback after that action and the route to help all need to feel connected.

items.title: Ineba Gogo MFB

caseStudy.role: Website Designer — responsible for the website’s visual design and interface layouts.
caseStudy.problem: Ineba Gogo Microfinance Bank needed a new website where prospective customers could find the business, understand its services, and learn how to open an account. The design needed to introduce the bank clearly and make its personal and business banking offerings easy to explore.
caseStudy.decisions:
I organised the content into distinct sections covering the bank, its services, its values, and its banking products. This gives visitors a clear path from learning about the business to exploring a relevant service.

The interface combines dark backgrounds, lighter content sections, and bright accents to distinguish information and highlight calls to action. Product cards separate personal and business banking, while icons support the service descriptions and values.

On mobile, the content follows a single-column layout with stacked cards and a compact navigation menu.
caseStudy.result: The new website gave people a place to discover the bank, understand what it offers, and find a route to opening an account. It established an online presence that supports both learning about the business and taking the next step towards becoming a customer.

items.title: Belema Fintech Website

sections.heading: The brief
sections.body:
Belema Fintech wanted its existing website to look better and feel more presentable, while showing the full range of its services and products.

My responsibility was the website’s design. The focus was on improving the visual presentation and organising information so visitors could understand the business and explore its offerings.

sections.heading: Giving the content a clear hierarchy
sections.body:
The design uses large headings to establish the main message, followed by supporting copy and smaller groups of information. In the services section, icons and short headings separate the company’s key benefits into distinct points.

Light backgrounds give the content room to breathe, while green accents and a colourful illustration connect the section to the brand. This creates a clear visual order for visitors scanning the page.

images.caption: The services section groups key benefits beneath a prominent heading, with supporting icons and an illustration.
images.alt: Belema Fintech services section with benefit descriptions on the left and a colourful infrastructure illustration on the right.

sections.heading: Introducing the business
sections.body:
The About page pairs a clear statement of what Belema does with a more detailed company introduction. The two-column layout separates the headline from the explanation, keeping each easy to scan.

A company-logo strip sits below the introduction, adding visual context to the business presentation without competing with the main message.

images.caption: The About page combines a bold introduction, supporting company information and a company-logo strip.
images.alt: Belema Fintech About page showing a large headline, company description and logos beneath the introduction.

sections.heading: Making products and contact details easy to find
sections.body:
The main navigation groups the website into familiar destinations: Home, About Us, Products, Resources and Contact Us.

The footer provides another route to the product pages and brings together company information, support links, contact details and office locations. Its dark green background and lime brand mark create a distinct ending to the page.

images.caption: The footer organises product links, company information and contact details into separate columns.
images.alt: Dark green Belema Fintech footer with product links, contact information, office addresses and social links.

sections.heading: The outcome
sections.body:
The redesigned website gave Belema Fintech a more polished presentation of its products, services and company information.

I also observed higher search rankings after launch. This is a qualitative observation; the case study does not attribute that improvement to visual design alone.

caseStudy.role: Website Designer — responsible for the visual design and interface layouts.
caseStudy.summary: I redesigned Belema Fintech’s website to give the business a more polished online presence and present its products and services clearly. The design brings together structured content, bold typography and the brand’s green palette to help visitors explore what the company offers.

items.description: A redesign of Belema Fintech’s website, giving its payment products and services a clearer, more professional presentation.

items.title: Food Couriers
items.description: A food-delivery app design bringing meal discovery, product details and order review into a connected mobile experience.

caseStudy.summary: Food Couriers is a client food-delivery app project I designed in Figma. The work explores the journey from browsing meals to reviewing an order, supported by research involving 20 participants. I delivered the completed interface designs to the client.

sections.heading: The brief
sections.body:
The project centred on a mobile food-delivery experience. The design needed to bring food discovery, meal information and order review into a connected journey.

My responsibility was the app's UI/UX design. I developed the interface screens and their visual presentation for delivery to the client.

sections.heading: Research and the core journeys
sections.body:
The research phase involved 20 participants. The project presentation also documented task flows for getting started with the app and placing a food order.

These flows frame the experience around two practical tasks: reaching the home screen and moving from selecting a meal to reviewing an order. The final screens show how those tasks connect across the app.

sections.heading: From browsing to choosing a meal
sections.body:
The home screen brings together the delivery location, search, food categories, promotional offers and meal cards. Images, prices and ratings give people information to compare while browsing.

The food-detail screen gives the selected meal more space, pairing a large image with its name, supporting information and a prominent action at the bottom. This creates a visual transition from exploring several options to considering one item.

images.caption: Meal discovery combines search, categories, offers and food cards.
images.alt: Food Couriers home screen with food categories, a promotional banner and meal cards.

images.caption: The detail screen brings the selected meal into focus.
images.alt: Food Couriers meal-detail screen with a large burger photograph and product information.

sections.heading: Reviewing the order and managing a profile
sections.body:
The order screen groups selected meals into separate rows with quantity controls. A summary area beneath the items brings the price breakdown and order action together.

The profile screen separates personal information from contact details and provides an edit action. Both screens use grouped information and clear headings to make their content easier to scan.

images.caption: Order review groups meal selections, quantities and a price summary.
images.alt: Food Couriers order screen showing three food items, quantity controls and an order summary.

images.caption: Profile information is organised into personal and contact sections.
images.alt: Food Couriers profile screen with an avatar, personal information, contact details and an edit button.

sections.heading: A consistent visual language
sections.body:
The interface combines pink and red accents with light backgrounds, rounded cards and food photography. Poppins typography provides a consistent style across headings, labels and supporting text.

Food illustrations and decorative line drawings give the app a recognisable character. Stronger accent colours draw attention to primary actions and selected navigation elements.

sections.heading: Delivery and reflection
sections.body:
I delivered the completed interface designs to the client, covering the welcome experience, meal discovery, food details, order review and profile management.

Looking back, my next iteration would focus on interface-copy consistency, accurate price calculations and task-based usability testing of the ordering flow. These checks would help refine the design before implementation.
